source.title: Renormalizable Spectral-Shell Dynamics as the Origin of Neural Scaling Laws

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives a conditional theoretical result about temporal non-monotonicity in test loss, using a spectral-shell argument rather than an empirical epoch sweep. It does not test the other claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: Section 6 derives a sufficient condition for non-monotone test loss and describes early amplification followed by eventual decay. The Pythia experiments measure spectral-shell energies, not test error across epochs, model sizes, or sample sizes, so those results are not rows for these versions. Statements about scaling and double descent cited from other work are also excluded.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper. Section 6 argues that, under assumed renormalizable power-law spectral transport (c0 > 0, decreasing initial spectrum), the finite-sample mismatch term in test loss can grow and then decay over training time. So test loss is non-monotone while training loss falls. This is a conditional mechanism, not a result on whether a version holds. No concrete model or setting is analysed to produce a test-error curve. Non-monotonicity is asserted to 'manifest as the classical double-descent curve', but the fall-rise-fall shape is not derived. The Pythia experiments (Sec. 7) measure spectral-shell energy profiles, not test error over epochs, model size or samples. The paper therefore discusses double descent and proposes an explanation without testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, with two refinements. The authors present a spectral-shell framework that, under renormalizability and effective power-law transport assumptions, they say explains both neural scaling laws and double descent. They attribute double descent to transport-induced amplification within an in-domain finite-sample mismatch window while training loss decreases monotonically. Their Pythia experiments validate only the assumed shell-energy structures, not double descent itself.
record.recipe_differences: No experimental reproduction of the original double-descent method; the paper develops a theoretical spectral-shell framework and reports spectral-shell measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The predicted non-monotonicity depends on the mismatch window intersecting a region with positive amplitude growth; the paper states that positive growth occurs when the initial spectrum is decreasing and c0 > 0.

fits_no_version.finding: Under assumed power-law spectral transport, the transport-induced amplitude A(λ,t) grows when c0 > 0 and the initial spectrum is decreasing. If that growth overlaps the finite-sample train/test mismatch window, test loss is non-monotone while training loss decreases (Sec. 6.3–6.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Epoch-wise test-loss non-monotonicity can arise from spectral transport interacting with in-domain finite-sample spectral mismatch (mechanistic account, conditional on assumptions).

record.problems: The temporal double-descent result is conditional on assumed spectral transport and finite-sample mismatch structure. The empirical Pythia analysis measures shell-energy profiles rather than test error across training time, model size, or sample size, and does not empirically validate the proposed double-descent mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version rows were omitted. Empirical shell-energy profiles and checkpoint/model comparisons in Sections 7.3–7.6 were left out because they do not measure test error or the named double-descent behavior.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep or derivation of test error versus size; Sec. 6.2 only asserts that capacity shifts the timing of the amplification.
No epoch-wise test-error curve is measured or explicitly derived; only a sufficient condition for non-monotonicity under assumed dynamics.
No sample-size analysis of test error; dataset size is said only to shift the mismatch window.
No capacity sweep or comparison across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Label noise, regularization and multiple peaks are not analysed.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a limits_scope label for V2 was downgraded. The paper never computes a test-error curve, theoretically for a concrete model or empirically, so there is no result on whether epoch-wise double descent holds or fails. The rows_left_out exclusion of the Pythia shell-energy results is correct. The Sec. 6.2 assertions that double descent does not rely on overparameterization, and that capacity or data size only shift its timing, are unsupported statements, not results.

versions.untested_parts: No model-size sweep measures test error or a peak near the training-set interpolation size.
The result is conditional and theoretical; no actual epoch sweep measures the complete fall-rise-fall test-error curve, including an initial decline and a peak.
No sample-size sweep measures whether adding training data raises test error near interpolation.
No comparison across model classes or capacity sweep tests a general double-descent curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across axes.
The paper does not test label-noise or regularization dependence, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
The paper does not compare the curve against an effective parameter count or test whether re-counting complexity makes it U-shaped.

rows.subject: renormalizable spectral-shell dynamics
rows.operation_detail: Derives a sufficient condition for temporal non-monotonicity of test loss from transport-induced amplitude growth and finite-sample spectral mismatch.

conditions.value: Mismatch window intersects a non-negligible region where the transport-induced amplitude grows
c0 > 0 and the initial spectrum is decreasing

rows.value: The test loss is necessarily non-monotone under the stated sufficient condition; early amplification is followed by eventual decay.
rows.note: This is a conditional theoretical implication, not an observed test-error curve. It establishes non-monotonicity under the stated assumptions but does not demonstrate the complete fall-rise-fall shape in a trained model.
rows.check: R1 is a conditional theoretical implication, not a measured or derived test-error curve for any specific model. It shows only that a mismatch-weighted term can rise and then decay under assumed transport. It does not establish the initial fall, a peak location, or a second descent. It bears on no version as a result. It is recorded under fits_no_version as a proposed mechanism.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Section 6 proposes a theoretical explanation of double descent, but establishes no complete trajectory or other result testing the specified versions.

tranche.reason: The conditional non-monotonicity argument does not establish V2's complete fall-rise-fall trajectory. The empirical measurements concern spectral-shell energies rather than any claim version's test-error curve.

source_check.notes: Section 6.4 explicitly asserts necessary non-monotonicity under its sufficient condition; R1 accurately records that assertion. This should not be treated as an observed or fully derived fall-rise-fall test-loss curve.

reader_labels.reason: The derived non-monotonicity is conditional on transport-induced amplitude growth overlapping the finite-sample mismatch window, and does not establish the full epoch-wise curve empirically (R1).
